title: Bond market tariffs
text:
I never really understood simple concepts related to bonds, yields, inflation, and exact role of the Federal Reserve.  All I knew was that bonds are "safer" than stocks, and they are inversely related (when stock market goes down investors flee to bonds and prices go up but yields go down).

So, the current phenomenon is puzzling in that bond prices are down (investors are dumping bonds, yields are going up) at the same time stocks and the dollar have fallen.  In order to better understand the relationship, I did a brief review. 

Simplified Relationships

â¢ Fed raises rates â T-bills up â Bond yields up, prices down â Stocks often down â Dollar stronger â Inflation moderated.
â¢ Inflation spikes â Fed tightens or raises rates â T-bills and bonds rise â Stocks falter â Dollar gains.
If unemployment spikes, Fed lowers rates.
â¢ Stocks soar â Risk appetite up â Bond demand down, bond prices fall but yields up â Dollar can weaken if Fed eases.

Key Players and Their Basics

1. Bonds: Debt instruments (e.g., U.S. Treasuries) where investors lend money to issuers (like the government) for a fixed return 
(yield). Prices move inversely to yields—when yields rise, prices fall.

2. Stocks: Equity shares in companies, reflecting ownership and growth expectations. Prices rise with optimism, fall with fear.

3. Dollar Strength: The U.S. dollar’s value against other currencies, tracked by indexes like DXY. Strong dollar = more buying power abroad.

4. Inflation: The rate at which prices for goods and services rise. High inflation erodes money’s value.

5. T-bill Rates: Yields on short-term U.S. Treasury securities (e.g., 3-month, 1-year). They’re “risk-free” benchmarks set by market demand and Fed policy.

6. Federal Reserve: The U.S. central bank, steering monetary policy via interest rates and money supply to balance inflation and growth.

How They Interconnect

1. Federal Reserve and T-bill Rates

â¢ The Fed sets the federal funds rate (overnight bank lending rate), which anchors T-bill rates. When the Fed hikes rates—say, from 4.25% to 4.5% in December 2024, per recent minutes—T-bill yields rise too (e.g., 3-month T-bills hit 4.6% in April 2025). Why? Investors demand higher returns as borrowing costs climb.
â¢ Mechanism: Open Market Operations—Fed buys T-bills to inject cash (lowering yields) or sells to tighten money (raising yields).

2. T-bill Rates and Bonds

â¢ T-bill rates ripple across the yield curve. Higher short-term rates push up longer-term Treasury yields (e.g., 10-year notes rose from 3.8% to 4.2% in Q1 2025). Bond prices drop as yields climb—$1,000 bonds paying 3% lose value when new ones offer 4%.
â¢ Inverse Link: Safe-haven demand can invert this; if stocks tank, investors flock to bonds, cutting yields despite Fed hikes.

3. Bonds and Stocks

â¢ Competition: Higher bond yields lure capital from stocks—why risk equities when T-bills pay 4.6%? In 2025, S&P 500 dipped 3% post-Fed hike as investors shifted to bonds.
â¢ Valuation: Rising yields increase discount rates for future cash flows, hammering growth stocks (e.g., tech). When 10-year yields hit 4.2%, Nasdaq fell 5% in a week.
â¢ Flight to Safety: If inflation spikes or recession looms, stocks crash, bonds rally—10-year yields dropped to 3.5% during 2020’s panic.

4. Inflation and Everything

â¢ Bonds: Inflation erodes fixed returns—5% inflation on a 4% bond means real losses. Investors demand higher yields (10-year spiked to 4.5% in mid-2024 as CPI hit 6%).
â¢ Stocks: Moderate inflation boosts profits (pricing power), but high inflation squeezes margins (input costs) and sparks rate hikes—Dow lost 8% in Q3 2024.
â¢ T-bills: Fed fights inflation with rate hikes, lifting T-bill yields. CPI eased to 3.2% by April 2025, but T-bills stayed elevated at 4.5%.
â¢ Dollar: Inflation weakens the dollar if unchecked (less purchasing power), but Fed tightening strengthens it—DXY rose 7% in 2025 as rates climbed.

5. Dollar Strength Ties It Together

â¢ Bonds: Strong dollar attracts foreign buyers to Treasuries, lowering yields—Japanese funds snapped up $20 billion in T-bills in Q1 2025.
â¢ Stocks: Strong dollar hurts exporters (Apple’s China sales dipped 4% in 2025) but boosts importers (Walmart gained 2%).
â¢ Inflation: Strong dollar curbs import costs (oil priced in USD fell 5% in April 2025), easing inflation pressure—CPI dropped 0.3% that month.
â¢ Fed: Dollar strength gives the Fed room to pause hikes; if too strong, it risks exports, nudging rate cuts—speculated for late 2025.

The Fed’s Balancing Act

â¢ Mandate: Stable prices (2% inflation target) and full employment. In 2025, with unemployment at 3.8% and inflation at 3.2%, the Fed’s hawkish—holding rates at 4.25â4.5%.
â¢ Tools: Rate hikes cool inflation but slow growth (GDP growth fell to 2.1% in Q1 2025). Quantitative tightening (selling $95 billion in bonds monthly) shrinks money supply, lifting yields.
â¢ Feedback Loop: Higher T-bill rates signal tighter policy, impacting bonds (yields up), stocks (growth down), dollar (stronger), and inflation (eased).
Real-World Example: 2025 Dynamics
â¢ Trump’s April 2 tariffs (20% on imports) spiked inflation fears—CPI ticked to 3.5%. Fed signaled no cuts, T-bill rates hit 4.6%, and 10-year yields rose to 4.3%. Stocks wobbled (S&P down 2%), the dollar surged (DXY to 108), and bond prices sagged. Investors bet on Fed tightening, but if tariffs tank growth, rate cuts could flip the script by Q4.

Bottom Line

These elements dance together, driven by the Fed’s hand on the wheel. Higher T-bill rates (Fed’s lever) lift bond yields, pressuring stocks and strengthening the dollar, which tames inflation. But external shocks—like tariffs or oil jumps—can scramble the rhythm. In 2025, the Fed’s juggling a strong dollar and tariff fallout, with markets hanging on every signal. It’s less a straight line, more a feedback loop where each piece nudges the others—sometimes in sync, sometimes at odds.

Trump says he wants a low interest rate (which makes borrowing easier to stimulate the housing market and the US economy), lower oil prices, a weaker dollar (which makes it more expensive for international travel with a dollar and makes US goods abroad more expensive and perhaps foreigners holding US debt less attractive?).  What the net-net is very difficult for me to understand!  

If there are any errors, please correct me as I am outside my wheelhouse!
